## Microsoft security models: research summary

Primary Microsoft or GitHub pages were fetched where noted. Items marked **(snippet)** rest only on search-result excerpts, so verify them before citing externally.

### 1. Secure Future Initiative (SFI)
- **Core idea:** Secure by design, secure by default, secure in operations. Themes are secure foundations, proactive defense, and future-ready security. Pillars named include culture, governance, principles, and engineering. ([Microsoft SFI July 2026 report](https://microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/10/securing-our-future-july-2026-progress-report-on-microsofts-secure-future-initiative))
- **Key controls and reported results:**
  - Engineering defaults stop 83% of pipelines from reaching unapproved package endpoints.
  - Cross-boundary credential isolation is at 98.7%.
  - Public access was revoked on more than 732,000 resources.
  - Phishing-resistant MFA covers 99.97% of user/device pairs.
  - I found no direct figure for secrets removal.
- **Mapping to coding agents:** Restrict the agent's package and network endpoints, isolate its credentials per boundary, and ship secure defaults in the pipeline templates rather than relying on each repo.

### 2. Privileged access
- **PIM approval workflow:** Roles can require approval for activation, with one or more delegated approvers. Approvers cannot approve their own requests, and service principals cannot approve. The first approver's decision resolves the request. The 24-hour approval window is fixed, and activation is time-bound. ([Microsoft Learn, PIM approval](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-approval-workflow))
  - Mapping: this is the model for Compliance's "named human approver." An agent identity must never be able to approve its own elevation.
- **Enterprise Access Model (snippet):** Three planes: control (former Tier 0), management (former Tier 1), and data/workload. Each plane controls the one below it. ([Microsoft Learn module](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/design-solutions-secure-privileged-access/2-enterprise-access-model))
  - Mapping: AWS Organizations/IAM Identity Center sit in the control plane, the infra management accounts in the management plane, and the HIPAA data stores in the data plane. Agents should not be able to modify the control plane.
- **Customer Lockbox (snippet):** The customer approves each Microsoft operator access request. Access is time-limited, auto-revokes, and is logged under a distinct operator identity. ([Microsoft Purview Customer Lockbox](https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/customer-lockbox-requests))
  - Mapping: a template for time-boxed, approved break-glass access to production.
- **JIT/JEA and PAW (snippet only):** I did not reach Microsoft's own PAW or JEA pages. A Microsoft tech community post gives the core PAW idea: a tier-0 admin keyboard is itself a tier-0 system. ([Microsoft tech community](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/coreinfrastructureandsecurityblog/securing-privileged-access-for-the-ad-admin-part-2/259167))
  - Mapping: JEA-style constrained commands fit a narrow, approved set of actions for an agent.

### 3. AI agents
- **Entra Agent ID (fetched):** Agents get their own identity type, separate from users and generic apps. ([Microsoft Learn, Agent ID authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/authorization-agent-id))
  - Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, and User Administrator cannot be assigned to agents.
  - Blocked Graph permissions include `RoleManagement.ReadWrite.All`, `User.ReadWrite.All`, and `Application.ReadWrite.All`. Even an administrator cannot consent to them.
  - Azure RBAC should be scoped to a single resource or resource group.
  - Custom roles can be assigned, which contradicts one secondary summary I saw.
- **Zero Trust for AI (snippet):** Microsoft's March 2026 framework and Agent 365 cover agent governance and visibility. Conditional Access for Agent ID is in preview. ([Microsoft Security Blog, March 2026](https://microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/19/new-tools-and-guidance-announcing-zero-trust-for-ai))
- **GitHub Copilot coding agent (fetched):** ([GitHub docs, risks and mitigations](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/risks-and-mitigations))
  - The agent pushes to a single branch: a `copilot/` branch, or the existing PR branch when triggered from a PR. It cannot push to main.
  - Internet access is restricted by a firewall.
  - Only users with write access can trigger it.
  - Workflows do not run until a writer reviews the agent's code, by default.
  - The agent cannot approve or merge a PR, and the requester cannot approve their own request.
  - Credentials are limited to simple push operations.
  - Built-in CodeQL and secret scanning run on its output.
  - Prompt injection remains a stated risk, mitigated by filtering hidden characters.

### What transfers to a small or mid-size company
- **Agents cannot grant themselves privilege.** Deny IAM-write and org-level actions to agent roles through permission boundaries or SCPs, and scope each agent to one account or resource. This mirrors Entra Agent ID's blocked-role list.
- **Make the human approval a platform gate, not a convention.** The agent's PR and any prod apply should need a named approver who is not the requester. Use environment protection rules for production and time-boxed elevation for break-glass. This satisfies Compliance directly.
- **Remove standing secrets and limit egress.** Prefer short-lived federated credentials for CI and agents over long-lived keys, and restrict agent network egress. This follows SFI's credential-isolation direction. The specific GitHub-to-AWS OIDC setup is my inference, not from these sources.
